concepts.name: Net vs. Gross Irrigated Area: Definitions and Measurement
key_dimensions: Distinction between Net Irrigated Area (NIA) and Gross Irrigated Area (GIA) — double-counting trap in GIA due to multiple crops per season
Why GIA can exceed NIA and how UPSC uses this to set MCQ traps on 'largest irrigated state'
India's current NIA (~68 million hectares) vs. irrigation potential created vs. irrigation potential utilized — the gap problem
Role of Agricultural Census and Land Use Statistics in reporting these figures

concepts.name: Sources of Irrigation: Canals, Tanks, Wells/Tubewells — Relative Share and Trends
key_dimensions: Historical dominance of canals (pre-independence) vs. current dominance of groundwater/tubewells (>60% of NIA) — reversal of trend
State-wise variation: canal dominance in Punjab/Haryana/UP vs. tank dominance in peninsular India (Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka)
Decline of tank irrigation — reasons (silting, encroachment, lack of maintenance, neglect of traditional systems)
UPSC trap: 'Groundwater is the largest source of irrigation in India' — True for current scenario but was not so at independence

concepts.name: Canal Irrigation: Types, Coverage, and Limitations
key_dimensions: Inundation canals vs. perennial canals — difference in source (flood-dependent vs. dam/weir-fed), reliability, and regional distribution
Command area vs. culturable command area (CCA) vs. gross command area (GCA) — definitional traps
Waterlogging and soil salinity as negative externalities of canal irrigation — affected states (Punjab, Haryana, UP, Rajasthan)
Canal irrigation best suited for: flat terrain, high water table areas — unsuitable for peninsular hard-rock terrain (key geographic linkage)

concepts.name: Tank Irrigation: Traditional System, Distribution, and Decline
key_dimensions: Geographic concentration in Deccan Plateau states — Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka — reasons (hard rock terrain, absence of perennial rivers)
Cascade tank systems in South India — interconnected series of tanks as traditional water harvesting
Reasons for decline: siltation, encroachment on tank beds/foreshore lands, poor maintenance post-zamindari abolition, neglect by state agencies
Revival efforts: MGNREGS for desilting tanks, Telangana's Mission Kakatiya, Tamil Nadu's Kudimaramathu scheme — policy linkage

concepts.name: Well and Tubewell Irrigation: Groundwater Exploitation and Regional Patterns
key_dimensions: Difference between open wells (phreatic/water table aquifer) and tubewells (deeper confined aquifers) — depth, reliability, and cost
Green Revolution's role in proliferation of tubewells — subsidized electricity as accelerant of groundwater depletion in Punjab, Haryana, Western UP
Critical groundwater-stressed states: Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan — CGWB classification of 'overexploited' blocks
UPSC trap: Tubewell irrigation is most prevalent in alluvial plains (Indo-Gangetic Plain) — NOT in peninsular hard-rock terrain where yields are low

concepts.name: Drip and Sprinkler Irrigation: Micro-Irrigation Systems
key_dimensions: Drip irrigation (trickle irrigation) vs. sprinkler irrigation — mechanism, water efficiency, suitable crops, and terrain
Per Drop More Crop (PDMC) — component under Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY); targets, funding (60:40 Centre-State), and coverage
Water use efficiency: Drip saves ~30–50% water vs. flood irrigation; sprinkler saves ~25–30% — frequently tested figures
State leaders in micro-irrigation: Maharashtra, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan — driven by water scarcity and horticulture crops

concepts.name: Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana (PMKSY): Architecture and Components
key_dimensions: Four components and their predecessor schemes: AIBP (Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme), HKKP (Har Khet Ko Pani), PDMC, Watershed Development (WDC-PMKSY) — merger trap
PMKSY's 'Har Khet Ko Pani' vs. 'More Crop Per Drop' — distinction in objectives (coverage expansion vs. efficiency improvement)
Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme (AIBP): focus on completing long-pending major/medium irrigation projects; 99 projects identified under PMKSY-AIBP
District Irrigation Plans (DIPs) and State Irrigation Plans (SIPs) as decentralized planning tools under PMKSY

concepts.name: Accelerated Irrigation Benefits Programme (AIBP): Purpose, Performance, and Issues
key_dimensions: Launched 1996-97 to provide central loan assistance for completion of incomplete major/medium irrigation projects — later converted to grants
CAG criticism: cost overruns, time overruns, irrigation potential created vs. utilized gap — accountability issues
UPSC trap: AIBP covers only major and medium irrigation projects — NOT minor irrigation; minor irrigation is state subject with different funding
Merger into PMKSY in 2015-16 — AIBP retained as a sub-scheme focusing on 99 prioritized incomplete projects

concepts.name: Major, Medium, and Minor Irrigation: Classification and Policy Implications
key_dimensions: Classification by Culturable Command Area (CCA): Major (>10,000 ha), Medium (2,000–10,000 ha), Minor (<2,000 ha) — exact thresholds are exam-critical
Constitutional and financial implications: Major/Medium are capital-intensive, centrally assisted; Minor irrigation largely state-funded and decentralized
Minor irrigation includes both surface (small tanks, diversion weirs) and groundwater (wells, tubewells) — often overlooked in exam answers
UPSC trap: Minor irrigation projects are more numerous but individually smaller; groundwater irrigation (tubewells) falls under minor irrigation category

concepts.name: Irrigation Potential Created vs. Irrigation Potential Utilized: The Utilization Gap
key_dimensions: Irrigation Potential Created (IPC) consistently exceeds Irrigation Potential Utilized (IPU) — gap of ~10–15 million hectares nationally
Reasons for gap: lack of field channels (last-mile connectivity), poor maintenance of distribution network, waterlogging, farmer behavior, crop choice mismatch
Command Area Development and Water Management Programme (CADWMP) — aimed at bridging this gap through field channels, land leveling, warabandi system
UPSC trap: Creating irrigation infrastructure does not guarantee utilization — efficiency and last-mile issues are separate policy problems

concepts.name: Warabandi System: Rotational Water Distribution in Canal Irrigation
key_dimensions: Definition: Fixed rotational schedule for equitable distribution of canal water among farmers in a distributary command area — time-based allocation
Prevalent in: Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan — associated with northwest Indian canal systems
Advantages: equity, predictability, reduced conflict; Limitations: rigid scheduling ignores crop water needs, tail-end farmers disadvantaged in practice
Comparison with volumetric pricing of water — warabandi is time-based NOT volume-based; UPSC may test this distinction in water governance questions

concepts.name: Groundwater Depletion and Over-Exploitation: Crisis Dimensions
key_dimensions: CGWB's classification: Safe, Semi-critical, Critical, Over-exploited blocks — over-exploited blocks concentrated in Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu
Green Revolution–groundwater nexus: MSP for water-intensive crops (paddy, wheat) + free electricity = structural incentive for over-extraction
Jal Shakti Abhiyan and Atal Bhujal Yojana (Atal Jal) — community-led groundwater management in water-stressed states; World Bank assisted
UPSC linkage: Groundwater depletion → food security risk (Punjab's agrarian crisis) → need for crop diversification (incentivizing maize, pulses in Punjab)

concepts.name: Traditional/Indigenous Irrigation Systems: Diversity and Revival
key_dimensions: System-wise geography: Karez/Kariz (underground channels) in Rajasthan/Balochistan; Phad system (Maharashtra); Ahar-Pyne (Bihar); Zabo (Nagaland); Surangam (Kerala/Karnataka)
Johad (Rajasthan) — earthen check dams; Rajendra Singh's Tarun Bharat Sangh revival — CSE/UPSC case study favorite
Common thread: community-managed, low-energy, ecologically sustainable — contrast with state-managed large canal systems
Policy relevance: MGNREGS, Jal Shakti Abhiyan use traditional water harvesting structures (TWHS) as implementation tools — convergence angle

concepts.name: Inter-State River Water Disputes and Irrigation Access
key_dimensions: Constitutional provision: Article 262 — Parliament may by law provide for adjudication of disputes relating to waters of inter-state rivers; excludes Supreme Court jurisdiction (UPSC trap)
Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956 — Tribunals: Cauvery (Tamil Nadu vs. Karnataka vs. Kerala vs. Puducherry), Krishna, Godavari, Mahanadi (Odisha vs. Chhattisgarh)
Cauvery Water Management Authority (CWMA) — set up after Supreme Court 2018 judgment; UPSC trap: SC CAN hear the matter if it involves constitutional interpretation, not just water sharing
Impact on irrigation: Unresolved disputes stall reservoir operation protocols, affecting sowing calendars and cropping patterns downstream

concepts.name: Irrigation and Cropping Pattern: Water-Intensive vs. Water-Efficient Crops
key_dimensions: Water footprint comparison: Paddy (~1,500–2,000 liters/kg) vs. Wheat (~900 liters/kg) vs. Millets (~300–500 liters/kg) — policy implication for crop shift
MSP regime perpetuating paddy-wheat monoculture in water-scarce Punjab and Haryana — structural market failure
Direct Seeded Rice (DSR) technology — saves ~15–20% water vs. transplanted paddy; being promoted by Punjab and Haryana governments
Nutri-cereals/Millets (IYOM 2023) as water-efficient alternatives — government push and its irrigation demand reduction potential

concepts.name: Irrigation Coverage and Regional Disparities: Irrigated vs. Rainfed Agriculture
key_dimensions: Only ~52% of India's net sown area is irrigated — ~48% remains rainfed; rainfed agriculture supports ~40% of food production and majority of pulses/oilseeds

Regional disparity: High irrigation intensity in Punjab (~98%), Haryana, UP vs. low in northeast, eastern India (Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Odisha) — 'Eastern India irrigation paradox' (abundant water, low irrigation)
Rainfed Area Development (RAD) sub-scheme under NMSA — integrated farming systems approach for rainfed areas
UPSC trap: Eastern India has abundant rainfall and river water but low irrigation due to lack of infrastructure, not water scarcity — different policy solution needed

concepts.name: Flood Irrigation vs. Precision Irrigation: Efficiency and Subsidy Distortions
key_dimensions: Flood/surface irrigation: most common (~75% of irrigated area), cheapest to operate, most wasteful (40–50% field application efficiency)
Drip: 80–90% efficiency; Sprinkler: 70–80% efficiency — UPSC may ask to rank these
Flat-rate/free electricity subsidy for agriculture as key barrier to efficiency — removes price signal for water conservation
Rationalization debate: Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) for electricity subsidy to farmers vs. current flat-rate subsidy — power sector–irrigation nexus

concepts.name: Command Area Development and Water Management Programme (CADWMP)
key_dimensions: Objective: Bridge IPC–IPU gap by developing field channels (chak channels), land leveling, on-farm development works in canal command areas
Now subsumed under PMKSY — institutional continuity but UPSC may test original standalone programme details
Water User Associations (WUAs) / Pani Panchayats — participatory irrigation management (PIM); transfer of canal management to farmer groups
UPSC trap: CADWMP focuses on last-mile connectivity WITHIN existing command areas — it does NOT create new irrigation potential; it improves utilization of already-created potential

concepts.name: Waterlogging and Soil Salinity/Alkalinity as Irrigation Externalities
key_dimensions: Mechanism: Excessive canal irrigation → rising water table → waterlogging → capillary rise of salts → secondary salinization; distinct from primary (natural) salinity
Affected area: ~6–8 million hectares under waterlogging/salinity/alkalinity in India; worst in canal-irrigated areas of Punjab, Haryana, UP, Rajasthan
Reclamation methods: Gypsum application (for alkaline/usar soils), sub-surface drainage, bio-drainage (eucalyptus plantations), laser land leveling
Policy linkage: This is a major argument for shifting from flood irrigation to drip/sprinkler; also linked to declining soil health and need for soil health cards

concepts.name: Interlinking of Rivers (ILR) and Its Irrigation Potential
key_dimensions: National Perspective Plan (NPP) by National Water Development Agency (NWDA): 30 links — 14 Himalayan + 16 Peninsular components; projected to irrigate additional ~35 million hectares
Ken-Betwa Link Project: First ILR project under implementation — benefits Bundelkhand (MP and UP); Panna Tiger Reserve controversy (environmental clearance issues)
UPSC trap: ILR is NOT a new idea — first proposed by Sir Arthur Cotton (for navigation), then M. Visvesvaraya; modern plan by Dr. K.L. Rao and Captain Dastur
Criticisms: Ecological disruption, displacement, inter-state consent challenges, questionable surplus-deficit basin calculations, high cost — balanced answer essential
